question: What is the meaning of material criticality in relation to sustainability?
description: Material criticality refers to the importance of a material in achieving sustainability goals, such as reducing waste and pollution. Materials with high criticality are those that are essential for circular economy practices, like recycling and reuse. They are often scarce, expensive, or have high environmental impact, making them crucial for sustainable construction and product design.

Introduction
The Earth’s natural resources are finite. Over 100 billion tonnes of resources are con-
sumed annually, leading to severe environmental and health issues, including approxi-
mately 9 million premature deaths from pollution [34]. This includes the annual produc-
tion of 300 million tonnes of plastic waste, 54 million tonnes of electronic waste, $460
billion worth of garment waste and a contribution of 45% of annual greenhouse gas emis-
sions – a figure that could potentially double by 2050 [39]. This immense consumption
and waste production puts tremendous pressure on virgin resources and landfill capacity.
The problem lies in the ‘once-through’ use of resources, where virgin materials are used
to produce things that end up in landfills. This is often described as a linear model. In
contrast, a circular model identifies and seeks to maximise restorative material flows that
recycle and reuse materials to reduce unrecoverable waste [14]. The Ellen MacArthur
Foundation emphasises two metrics for circularity [14]:
• The Material Circularity Indicator (MCI) measures the proportion of material
forming a restorative flow.
• The Linear Flow Index (LFI) measures the proportion of material ending as unre-
coverable waste.
Figure 1 illustrates these concepts and shows how the restorative part of the flow creates
a closed loop after old products reach the end of their lives.

The MCI has been shown to create opportunities for value in construction [23]. Central
to enabling circularity is the idea of material passports [7, 8] – digital documents that
provide detailed information about the composition, origin, and life cycle of materials in
products. The use of digital material passports is set to be mandated in the EU in the near
future [3, 51]. However, the lack of standardisation and interoperability of current mate-
rial passports presents a significant challenge to stakeholders. Material passports lack a
unified structure across industries and applications, posing data consistency and integra-
tion challenges. Furthermore, noisy data present a challenge in accurately calculating the
MCI and LFI.

In conclusion, these set of characterizing elements have been formed 
to develop the following formulation of the intensional definition: 
Definition: a material passport (or product passport) is a digital 
interface composing a certified identity of a single identifiable product 
by accessing the set of life cycle registrations linked to this object in 
order to yield insight into the sustainability and circularity character­
istics, the circular value estimation, and the circular opportunities for 
both that product and its underlying components and materials. 
4.2. Positioning the role of passports for strategizing circularity decisions 
in supply chain management 
The step succeeding the concept definition is to make generalizations 
and extract theory from our findings to fuel the academic debate on 
passports. Considering the objectives, boundaries, relationships, attri­
butes, stakeholders and challenges studied in this paper, we derived a 
holistic understanding of the role of passports for strategizing circularity 
decisions. This role can best be explained through Fig. 7, which shows 
the key components of the passport, their key relationships among them, 
and how these work together for achieving the passport objectives with 
respect to CSCM performance measurement. 
In consideration of the three passport objectives, the key architec­
tural challenge is to support flexible virtual replication of passport data 
for the creation of scenarios that help to evaluate how product changes 
affect circularity. In order to support such ’scenario exploration’ 
through passports, we suggest to represent data into four main compo­
nents. Each component consists of configurable features which can to be 
linked to the other main components. The main components can be 
easily replicated and altered to create new scenario’s while the under­
lying links to other main objects or object features are preserved. Such 
linked-component driven architecture reduces the creation complexity 
of scenarios for two reasons: (1) data can be managed by its responsible 
stakeholder, and (2) alternations only need to be applied locally (within 
the component) while outcomes can be evaluated under the full scenario 
context. Potentially, one may even subdivide these suggested compo­
nent structure into sub-components that again can be linked (e.g., 
product variations may be composed of different components). The four 
suggested components are: 
1. Product variations: The aim is to register for every single iden­
tifiable product the current and historical composition of components, 
materials and its associated characteristics. To facilitate scenario 
modelling, a flexibility is needed that supports creation of product 
variations that are the result of potential alternative compositions 
(different materials or component use). Such scenario creation helps for 
example in circular design and as part of suggested maintenance 
activities. 
2. Supply chain variations: The aim is to create variations in the 
supply chain configuration and see how these affects circularity. Ex­
amples include: to implement alternative processing technologies, 
switch from supplier or transport carrier, or introduce new forms of 
reverse logistics. 
3. Environmental impact variations: The aim is to select and 
compare different types of data sources and calculation methods to be 
used in the sustainability- and circularity-metrics of a single identifiable 
product. An end user may compare the different reference materials 
from various impact databases (e.g., ecoinvent or ecocost) since this 
reference material can vary because of scope, functional unit, context, 
size of application, etc. Alternatively, firms may wish to rely on more 
accurate firm-based data or real-time IoT-based data. Furthermore, 
calculation methods can have an effect on the calculated impact, hence, 
impact variations may be dependent on, for example, the used methods 
in defining impact categories (e.g., climate change) and the character­
ization of these impacts (e.g., GWP500). 
4. Sustainability and circularity metric variations: The aim is to 
create different selections of metrics that are relevant to the context of 
the product in the supply chain (e.g., product type, sales market, pro­
duction process, scale, socio-polical climate, etc.). The framework of 
Moraga et al. (2019) provides guidance how these metrics (e.g.,
